title: Stolen Focus: Why You Can't Pay Attention, and How to Think Deeply Again
source_note: Book itself not read. Guardian, Blinkist, SuperSummary fetches were blocked (403/429). Facts come from Wikipedia, the book's own site, a catalogue blurb and a review. Detail is thin; stories stay short and low-to-medium confidence.

facts.claim: Stolen Focus (Bloomsbury, 2022) argues that the modern attention crisis comes from systemic forces and not only from individual failure; it is organised into 12 deeper causes.
Hari describes a digital detox in Provincetown, Massachusetts: a beach house, a flip phone that could not get online, and a printed road map instead of a phone for navigating.
The Provincetown stay lasted three months, alone and screen-free, according to one review (the Wikipedia page gives no duration).
Hari reports first feeling agitated; the longer he stayed away the easier it became to clear his mind and stay with one task; letting his mind wander brought new ideas.

The book's own site and publisher material cite a reported figure of about 65 seconds of focus on one task for US college students and about three minutes for office workers. The page says 'reportedly'; scope and original study not confirmed.

Hari argues apps and social media are designed to capture and hold attention; he cites Facebook and YouTube as platforms that maximise screen time to collect personal data and drive recommendations and longer engagement.
The book features Silicon Valley dissidents who figured out how to hack human attention.

Among the twelve causes are physical and mental exhaustion, constant interruption by smartphones, switching between tasks (multitasking is described as ineffective and wearing), the decline of mind-wandering, and pollution.

The book also features veterinarians who diagnose dogs with ADHD, a favela in Rio where everyone lost attention in an unusual way, and an office in New Zealand that found a technique to restore workers' attention.
Always-on work culture and constant availability are argued to cause stress and lower productivity.

Hari's proposals are collective: regulating tech companies, treating attention as a public health issue, limits on internet use, shorter working hours (a four-day week is mentioned), more play away from screens for children, reading literature, caring for physical health. He calls it an 'attention rebellion'.
The book draws on over 250 interviews with experts in neuroscience, psychology, education and technology.
